label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
@Mikaela yes, we started 10 in 7 on 21 September, after mating had started. We’ve got 290 cows, mostly three-way crossbreds. We skip Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday arvos, plus Sunday arvo, so that’s four once-a-day milkings a week. Morning milking is 5.15 every day.

The honest production answer is that milksolids are down about 6% on the same weeks last year, going off the Fonterra app. Our rep had told us to expect 8–10%, so it’s been better than that here, but 6% is still 6%. It’s only my comparison for these weeks, not a proper trial or a full-season result, so I wouldn’t bank on getting exactly the same, particularly if you’re starting after Christmas rather than in spring.

Cells did go up. We went from about 110,000 to around 180,000 over the first three weeks, and we’re back around 135,000 now. We also had a heifer with mastitis go bad on a skipped arvo. We didn’t pick her up until the next morning and she lost a quarter. I won’t gloss over that one, because it was awful and it’s the sort of thing that can happen when you’re not seeing them at that second milking. You have to be really on your game with teat spraying and checking the cows properly on the skip days. If you get slack with that side of it, it’ll bite you.

The cows themselves came round much quicker than I expected. There were about four days of them bellowing at the gate and then they were fine.

Lameness has been a big plus. We’ve got four on the lame list now compared with 11 at this time last year. Our longest walk to the back paddocks is 1.8km, so taking those arvo trips out has made a noticeable difference here.

The people side has been just as noticeable. Kieran, our 2IC, said it’s the first spring he hasn’t wanted to quit by October. On our first skipped Sunday arvo, Dave and I went to Hamilton to see the grandkids. It was the first proper Sunday arvo off in spring we’d had in 20-odd years, which is a bit sad when you say it out loud.

So for us, honestly, I wouldn’t go back. The hours alone are worth the 6% hit to us. But that’s my call for my farm, not me saying everyone should wear it. The drop in production is real, the early cell count rise was real, and losing that heifer’s quarter was real. You’d need to be comfortable with those risks and keep on top of the checks, not just look at the extra time off.

If Tom’s knees are stuffed, the arvos off will help him more than anything. And from what Kieran’s been like, I can see why it might help with your young fella too, but I can’t tell you whether the numbers will stack up for your place.

Come and find me at the field day on the 19th and I’ll have the shed rosters and my production and cell count numbers with me. You’re welcome to look through the lot, warts and all. Or just ring me if you want to talk it through before then — much easier than me trying to text!
